data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Leg ulcers** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. Define a chronic leg ulcer.**
- Loss of skin below the knee (leg or foot) that does not heal within 4–6 weeks

**Q2. Classify leg ulcers by cause (PYQ).**
- Vascular: venous (70–80%), arterial (10–15%), mixed arteriovenous, lymphatic, vasculitic (PAN, rheumatoid, cryoglobulinaemia, ANCA), microthrombotic (antiphospholipid, livedoid vasculopathy, calciphylaxis, cholesterol emboli)
- Neuropathic (trophic): diabetes, leprosy, spinal disorders, alcohol, tabes dorsalis
- Infective: tropical ulcer, ecthyma, mycobacterial (TB, Buruli, leprosy), deep fungal (mycetoma, sporotrichosis), leishmaniasis, syphilis (gumma), yaws
- Haematological: sickle-cell disease, thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, polycythaemia, dysproteinaemias
- Neoplastic: SCC (Marjolin's ulcer in chronic scars), BCC, melanoma, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma
- Others: pyoderma gangrenosum, necrobiosis lipoidica, trauma, burns, dermatitis artefacta, drugs (hydroxyurea — malleolar ulcers), radiation, panniculitis

**Q3. Describe the venous drainage of the lower limb (PYQ).**
- Superficial veins: great saphenous (from medial end of dorsal arch, anterior to medial malleolus, along medial leg and thigh to saphenofemoral junction 3–4 cm below and lateral to pubic tubercle) and small saphenous (behind lateral malleolus, up the back of calf to popliteal vein)
- Deep veins: paired venae comitantes of anterior/posterior tibial and peroneal veins → popliteal → femoral → external iliac
- Perforators connect superficial to deep with valves directing flow inwards (Cockett's medial ankle perforators, Boyd's below knee, Dodd's/Hunter's in thigh)
- Calf muscle pump: contraction compresses deep veins and pushes blood upwards; valves prevent reflux — failure gives ambulatory venous hypertension

**Q4. Explain the pathogenesis of venous ulcers.**
- Valvular incompetence (primary, or post-thrombotic) and calf pump failure → sustained ambulatory venous hypertension → capillary distension and leakage of fibrinogen, RBCs → pericapillary fibrin cuffs (oxygen diffusion barrier hypothesis), leucocyte trapping (white cell trapping hypothesis), growth-factor trapping, MMP activity → tissue hypoxia, inflammation and ulceration

**Q5. Describe the clinical features of a venous ulcer and its associated signs.**
- Site: gaiter area — above the medial malleolus (commonest), shallow, irregular sloping edges, granulation tissue and fibrinous slough, moderate exudate; mild pain relieved by elevation
- Surrounding changes: varicose veins, oedema, haemosiderin pigmentation (brown), stasis (venous) eczema, lipodermatosclerosis (inverted champagne-bottle leg), atrophie blanche (white stellate scars with telangiectasia), corona phlebectatica (ankle flare)
- CEAP classification: C0 none — C1 telangiectasia/reticular — C2 varicose veins — C3 oedema — C4 skin changes (a pigmentation/eczema, b LDS/atrophie blanche, c corona phlebectatica) — C5 healed ulcer — C6 active ulcer

**Q6. Differentiate venous, arterial and neuropathic ulcers.**
- Venous: gaiter area, shallow, irregular, exudative, mild pain eased by elevation, pulses present, warm, oedema, pigmentation
- Arterial: distal pressure points (toes, heel, shin, lateral malleolus), punched-out, deep, dry pale/necrotic base, severe pain worse on elevation and at night, absent pulses, cold shiny hairless skin, intermittent claudication, ABPI <0.8
- Neuropathic: pressure points of sole (metatarsal heads, heel), punched-out painless with callus rim, sensory loss, warm foot with pulses (unless mixed diabetic), deformity (Charcot joint)

**Q7. Discuss the evaluation of a leg ulcer.**
- History: duration, pain, DVT, varicose veins, diabetes, smoking, trauma, drugs, systemic disease
- Examination: site, size (measure/photograph), edge, base, discharge, surrounding skin, pulses, sensation, joints
- Ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI) with hand-held Doppler: 0.9–1.3 normal; <0.8 arterial disease (avoid high compression); <0.5 severe ischaemia; >1.3 calcified vessels (diabetes — use toe pressures)
- Venous duplex ultrasound (reflux, obstruction); arterial duplex/angiography if ABPI low
- Bloods: CBC, sugar/HbA1c, renal function, albumin, ESR/CRP, lipid profile, autoimmune screen (ANA, ANCA, RF, cryoglobulins, APLA) when vasculitic
- Swab culture only if clinically infected; biopsy from edge if atypical, non-healing >3 months (SCC), PG/vasculitis suspected; X-ray/MRI for osteomyelitis

**Q8. Management of venous ulcers.**
- Compression therapy — cornerstone: multilayer bandage systems (4-layer, 2-layer short-stretch) delivering ~40 mmHg at ankle if ABPI ≥0.8; reduced compression if ABPI 0.5–0.8; then compression stockings class II–III lifelong to prevent recurrence
- Leg elevation, walking/calf exercises, weight loss
- Wound bed preparation (TIME — Tissue debridement, Infection/inflammation control, Moisture balance, Edge advancement): sharp/autolytic/enzymatic/larval debridement; appropriate dressings (hydrocolloid, foam, alginate for exudate, hydrogel for dry, silver/iodine for infection)
- Pentoxifylline 400 mg TDS (improves healing), micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF), aspirin (limited evidence)
- Treat stasis eczema with topical steroid (avoid sensitisers — check patch test), treat infection with systemic antibiotics
- Surgery: endovenous ablation of superficial reflux (EVLA, radiofrequency, foam sclerotherapy) — reduces recurrence (EVRA trial); split-thickness skin grafting, pinch grafts, cellular/tissue-based skin substitutes, PRP, NPWT for large ulcers

**Q9. What is Marjolin's ulcer?**
- Aggressive SCC arising in a chronic ulcer or scar (burns, venous ulcers, osteomyelitis sinus, DLE, lupus vulgaris); suspect with raised everted edge, bleeding, rapid growth, failure to heal — biopsy

**Q10. What is the TIME concept?**
- Framework for wound bed preparation: T — non-viable Tissue removal; I — Infection/Inflammation control; M — Moisture balance; E — Edge of wound (non-advancing/undermined) — later extended to TIMERS (Regeneration, Social factors)

**Q11. Write short notes on Milroy disease (PYQ).**
- Primary congenital lymphoedema (type I) — autosomal dominant FLT4 (VEGFR-3) mutation; bilateral lower-limb lymphoedema at or soon after birth, upslanting toenails, prominent veins, papillomatosis, hydrocele; lymphoscintigraphy shows absent uptake; treated with compression, skin care, prevention of cellulitis
- Other primary lymphoedema: Meige disease (lymphoedema praecox, puberty), lymphoedema tarda (>35 y), lymphoedema–distichiasis (FOXC2)

**Q12. Describe the arterial ulcer and peripheral arterial disease assessment.**
- Risk: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, age; claudication → rest pain → tissue loss (Fontaine/ Rutherford stages)
- Ulcer: punched-out, deep, pale/ necrotic base, little granulation, on toes, heel, lateral malleolus, shin; cold, pale, hairless shiny skin, thickened nails, absent pulses, delayed capillary refill, Buerger's test (pallor on elevation, rubor on dependency)
- ABPI <0.9 PAD, <0.5 critical; toe pressure <30 mmHg poor healing; duplex/ CT angiography; refer for revascularisation; no compression if ABPI <0.5

**Q13. Describe the diabetic foot ulcer and its classification.**
- Neuropathic (painless, plantar pressure points, callus), ischaemic, or neuro-ischaemic; infection and Charcot foot complicate
- Wagner grading: 0 at-risk foot, 1 superficial ulcer, 2 deep ulcer to tendon/ capsule, 3 deep with abscess/ osteomyelitis, 4 forefoot gangrene, 5 whole-foot gangrene; also University of Texas classification (grade + stage — infection/ ischaemia)
- Management: offloading (total contact cast), debridement, infection control (probe-to-bone test — osteomyelitis), glycaemic control, revascularisation, footwear education

**Q14. What is the role of compression — types and pressure?**
- Elastic (long-stretch) bandages/ stockings — high resting pressure; inelastic (short-stretch) bandages/ Unna boot — high working pressure, low resting pressure (better tolerated, good with calf pump)
- Multilayer systems (4-layer: orthopaedic wool, crepe, elastic, cohesive) deliver ~40 mmHg at ankle; stockings — class I (14–17 mmHg), II (18–24, UK) / 20–30 (international), III (25–35) / 30–40 mmHg
- Contraindications: ABPI <0.5–0.6, severe heart failure, severe neuropathy (caution), acute DVT (relative), skin infection

**Q15. Discuss dressings for leg ulcers.**
- Choose by exudate and wound bed: hydrogels (dry/ sloughy — autolytic debridement), hydrocolloids (low–moderate exudate), foams (moderate–heavy exudate), alginates/ hydrofibre (heavy exudate, bleeding), antimicrobial — silver, iodine, honey, PHMB (critical colonisation), non-adherent contact layers (paraffin gauze, silicone); change frequency by exudate
- Avoid sensitisers (lanolin, neomycin, fragrance) — ulcer patients have high contact allergy rates

**Q16. Pyoderma gangrenosum as a cause of leg ulcer — clues.**
- Rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with violaceous undermined border, purulent base, starts as pustule, pathergy (worsens after debridement/ surgery), cribriform scarring; associations — IBD, arthritis, haematological malignancy (myeloma, leukaemia), PAPA
- Diagnosis of exclusion (PARACELSUS/ Delphi criteria); biopsy edge to exclude infection/ vasculitis/ malignancy; treat with systemic steroids, cyclosporine, TNF inhibitors (infliximab), IVIG, topical tacrolimus/ steroids; avoid surgical debridement

**Q17. Haematological ulcers — which and why?**
- Sickle cell disease (malleolar ulcers — vaso-occlusion, haemolysis), thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, polycythaemia vera, thrombocytosis, cryoglobulinaemia, cryofibrinogenaemia, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C/S deficiency — painful ulcers, often around ankles; check CBC, peripheral smear, Hb electrophoresis, thrombophilia screen

**Q18. What is Martorell's ulcer?**
- Hypertensive ischaemic leg ulcer — very painful necrotic ulcer on the lateral/ posterolateral distal leg (often over Achilles) in elderly with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension (and diabetes); arteriolosclerosis with medial calcification; pulses present; treat with BP control, debridement, split-skin grafting (best), pain control

**Q19. Calciphylaxis — features.**
- Calcific uraemic arteriolopathy in end-stage renal disease (and non-uraemic — warfarin, hyperparathyroidism): extremely painful violaceous retiform purpura → necrotic ulcers on thighs, abdomen, legs; high mortality (sepsis); biopsy shows vascular calcification and thrombosis; treat with sodium thiosulphate IV, stop warfarin/ calcium/ vitamin D, cinacalcet/ parathyroidectomy, wound care, hyperbaric oxygen

**Q20. Neuropathic ulcer in leprosy — management.**
- Plantar ulcer over metatarsal heads/ heel due to anaesthesia, dryness, autonomic loss, deformity; rest and offloading (no walking on ulcer), cleaning and dressing, treat infection, below-knee plaster cast for non-healing simple ulcers, protective MCR footwear with insoles, self-care (soak, scrape, oil), surgery for complicated ulcers (osteomyelitis — sequestrectomy)

**Q21. What investigations confirm osteomyelitis under an ulcer?**
- Probe-to-bone test (positive predicts osteomyelitis in diabetic foot), plain X-ray (periosteal reaction, bone destruction — late), MRI (most sensitive), ESR/CRP, bone biopsy for culture and histology (gold standard)

**Q22. Newer advanced therapies for chronic ulcers.**
- Negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT/ VAC), autologous platelet-rich plasma/fibrin, growth factors (becaplermin — PDGF), bioengineered skin substitutes (Apligraf, Dermagraft), amniotic membrane, epidermal grafting, hyperbaric oxygen (diabetic foot), electrical stimulation, larval (maggot) debridement therapy, ultrasound debridement

**Q23. What lifestyle advice for venous ulcer patients?**
- Lifelong compression stockings, leg elevation above heart level when resting, regular walking and ankle exercises, weight reduction, avoid prolonged standing/ sitting, skin moisturisation, stop smoking, early review if skin changes or injury

**Q24. Differential diagnosis of an ulcer with raised everted edge.**
- SCC (Marjolin's ulcer), BCC (rolled pearly edge), keratoacanthoma, melanoma (amelanotic), lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, deep fungal infection (chromoblastomycosis, sporotrichosis), tuberculosis (verrucous), leishmaniasis — biopsy the edge

**Q25. Vasculitic ulcer — clues.**
- Multiple, painful, punched-out ulcers with surrounding palpable purpura, livedo racemosa, nodules; systemic symptoms; RA/ SLE/ PAN/ cryoglobulinaemia/ ANCA vasculitis; biopsy (deep, edge) + DIF; treat underlying vasculitis with immunosuppression

**Q26. What is the role of systemic drugs in venous ulcer healing?**
- Pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily (reduces leucocyte activation, improves microcirculation) — improves healing with or without compression; micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF/ diosmin) — adjunct; aspirin — evidence weak; zinc only if deficient; antibiotics only for clinical infection

**Q27. Prognosis and recurrence.**
- ~50–70% of venous ulcers heal by 12–24 weeks with good compression; recurrence 30–70% in 1 year without stockings and venous surgery; poor prognostic factors — large (>10 cm²), long duration (>6 months), ABPI <0.8, immobility, obesity, deep vein reflux/ post-thrombotic syndrome

## Quick spotter facts
- Gaiter-area shallow ulcer + pigmentation + LDS — venous ulcer
- ABPI <0.8 — no high compression
- Non-healing ulcer with rolled edge — biopsy for Marjolin's SCC

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Leg ulcers, venous disease). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
